subject: A230B24E88D943A79A527E42B4172FE0
introduction: The writings of Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá inherit the language of Persian mystical poetry, in which the love of God is fire, the lover a moth, separation the one sorrow, and the Beloved’s cruelty a favour. This guide gathers that language: lines of verse quoted in the Seven Valleys, prayers of longing, letters of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá to those “enkindled”, and the daring remark, with which it opens, that at the last station even love is a veil. The Song of Songs and the Psalms of thirst are scripture’s share in the same language; Rúmí’s reed, Sa‘dí’s moth, Rábi‘ah and Ibn ‘Arabí are its Muslim classics; Augustine, Donne, Herbert and Thompson its Christian ones. The Buddha’s poisoned arrow, Herbert’s courteous Love and Theseus on lunatics and lovers each look at the pain of love differently.
questions: Why should love of God be described as pain at all? What would be missing from an account that left the pain out?
The readings call the Beloved’s “poison” sweet. How is that different from welcoming suffering for its own sake?
God hides, in reading 32; in Thompson the soul hides. Which matches your experience of seeking?
What might it mean that “love is a veil”?
This language comes from poetry. How literally do the readings mean it, and how should it be prayed?

outside.why: A realm of pure awareness where “not even love can find a way”. Paul placed love last and highest: now abideth faith, hope, charity; the greatest of these is charity. What could lie beyond love, in the reading’s scheme, and would Paul have recognized it?
Consumed each night by the fire of separation. As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.
Through divine love every bitterness becomes sweet. Love is strong as death; many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.
“Love is a veil betwixt the lover and beloved.” Rábi‘ah wanted nothing between, not even reward: if I worship Thee in hope of Paradise, exclude me from Paradise; Thou art enough for me.
The moth loves the light though its wings burn. Sa‘dí: learn love from the moth, because it burnt, lost its life, and found no voice.
Pass beyond the heart to the Beloved of hearts. You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in You.
Love requires a man to sacrifice his life and accept disgrace. Whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it.
The fish is never sated with water, nor the lover with the beloved. My soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land.
No patience in separation. My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the Lord: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God.
The fire of separation after the comfort of union. I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: I sought him, but I could not find him.
Nearness consumed, distance burned. Dickinson: parting is all we know of heaven, and all we need of hell.
“Love’s fool am I.” Socrates in the Phaedrus: the madness of love is the greatest of heaven’s blessings.
Worn from separation. Rúmí’s reed-flute: ever since they tore me from my osier bed, my plaintive notes have moved men and women to tears.

Love was ever rebellious and bloodthirsty, to put the outsider to flight. Shakespeare’s test of the genuine: love is not love which alters when it alteration finds; it looks on tempests and is never shaken.
The medicine of the yearning one is poison from the Beloved’s hand. Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.
In love with both His love and His wrath. Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth.

Take the poison as honey, and find a remedy in every pain. The Buddha’s parable of the man struck by a poisoned arrow treats pain as something to be removed at once, without speculation. Is suffering in these readings to be cured or to be cherished?
The world compounded of honey and colocynth. Keats: in the very temple of Delight veil’d Melancholy has her sovran shrine.
It hath stung the hearts of those who sought Thy nearness. How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?
Distracted by the countenance of the Beloved, she wandered. By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.
God kindles yearning and conceals Himself. Francis Thompson told it the other way round: the soul flees, and the Lover pursues down the nights and down the days. Who hides from whom?
Kindled with love, then forbidden the sight. My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me?

The lover must weep while the Beloved glances coyly away. Herbert’s Love is all courtesy: Love bade me welcome, yet my soul drew back; quick-ey’d Love drew nearer to me, sweetly questioning if I lack’d anything. Which picture of the divine Beloved do you recognize, the elusive or the welcoming?
The cup of death among Thy greatest bounties. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
Among the requirements of love are trials, blame and taunts. Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you.
The arena of self-annihilation. Donne: batter my heart, three-person’d God; o’erthrow me, and bend your force to break, blow, burn, and make me new.

“I have become mad, homeless and shelterless.” Theseus classes the lover with the lunatic and the poet, all of imagination compact. Is the madness in these readings a state to be sought, a figure of speech, or a risk?
Eyes turned white from flowing tears. My tears have been my meat day and night, while they continually say unto me, where is thy God?
The hearts of Thy lovers pierced by the arrows of separation. Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.
The mysteries of the love of God are hidden in the heart. Ibn ‘Arabí: I follow the religion of Love: whatever way Love’s camels take.
But for adversity, how could I taste Thy tenderness? We glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience.
The lover has no sorrow save separation. ’Tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all.
A closing prayer by the hearts set ablaze. Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.

shortfall: The readings between 36 and 71 are largely prayers of longing in one voice and image, fire and tears; companions were given where the image changes and not to each prayer.

song-my-beloved-had-withdrawn-himself.text: I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer. The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me. I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love
